entries.claim: On its Q1 FY2026 call (23 Jul 2026) Albertsons reaffirmed AI as "foundational" and guided FY26 capex of $1.9-2.0bn toward store modernization and AI capabilities, but disclosed no AI-attributed revenue metric. The 10% Ask AI basket-size lift CEO Susan Morris put on the record on the 7 Jan 2026 call was not repeated. Digital sales grew 13%, not attributed to AI.
entries.source_name: Q1 FY2026 earnings call, complete transcript (prior claim: Q3 FY2025 call, 7 Jan 2026, via PYMNTS / CX Today)
entries.mechanism: Ask AI conversational search in the Albertsons/Safeway/Vons/Jewel-Osco mobile apps surfaces complementary items mid-search, expanding the basket; household-level personalized offers on top of ~tens of millions of loyalty households. The mechanism is real and the January number was specific; what is missing is any repeat measurement.
entries.shape_justification: S2, and counter-evidence to it. Basket expansion inside an existing customer base buying existing groceries in existing stores - absent the AI, these shoppers buy groceries from somebody. Zero-sum at industry level, GDP-neutral. Logged as counter-evidence because the only quantified revenue-side AI metric this company had ever disclosed vanished from the next disclosure while AI capex was reaffirmed and expanded. Four named enterprise AI priorities were given (digital CX, merchandising intelligence, labor optimization, supply chain optimization); three of the four are cost-side, and the revenue-side one carried no number.
entries.falsifier: Reverse-falsifier: if Albertsons re-discloses the Ask AI basket-size lift, or any successor revenue-attributed AI metric at or above 10%, on the Q2 FY2026 call (expected Oct 2026), this entry is a reporting artifact and should be downgraded. If two more quarters pass with AI capex reaffirmed and still no AI-attributed revenue number, treat the January figure as a one-off marketing disclosure rather than a managed KPI.
entries.confidence_why: Absence-of-evidence is weaker than a stated walk-back; the July transcript was read via a summarizing fetch, so a passing mention could have been missed. The January 10% figure is Tier C reporting (two independent outlets) of a Tier A call, not the transcript itself.

entries.company: S&P 500 (510 firms, 2016-2025) - MIT FutureTech / CMU study
entries.claim: Peer-style study of AI adoption in 510 S&P 500 firms, scored from SEC 10-K language: in 2025 only 11% had AI "deeply integrated into their business processes", plus a further 10% "using AI in the production of goods and delivery of services", up from 5% in 2022. The technology sector "accounts for two-thirds of deeply integrated enterprise adoption", with only "slowly accelerating adoption among non-technology firms". Profitability follows a J-curve from no adoption to deep adoption, but the authors "observe no differences in capex or productivity".
entries.source_name: Yu, Fleming, Hampton, Combemale & Thompson, "AI Adoption in S&P 500 Firms", arXiv 2607.08920 (submitted 9 Jul 2026)
entries.mechanism: Not a deployment finding - a measurement of the population this log samples from. Adoption is scored off 10-K language, which sits under liability for materially false statements, so it is a harder measure than survey self-report. The finding that matters here is the denominator: two-thirds of genuinely deep enterprise AI adoption sits inside the technology sector, i.e. inside the population METHOD excludes as subjects.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence, tagged to S2 because S2 is where the bulk of revenue-attribution claims live, but it cuts against S3 equally. A J-curve in profitability with no measured productivity or capex difference is a margin story, not a top-line story; the paper finds no top-line effect to report. Directly bears on why this log's positive column is empty: the non-tech incumbents it tracks are precisely the slow-adopting tail, so scarce revenue disclosure may reflect thin real adoption rather than adoption without payoff. Those are very different worlds and this study does not separate them.
entries.falsifier: If a later vintage of this measure (2026-27 10-Ks) shows non-tech deep adoption converging toward tech-sector levels while revenue-side disclosure stays absent, the 'thin adoption' explanation dies and 'adoption without top-line payoff' is the live one. If non-tech deep adoption stays under ~10% of firms, this log should expect a structurally empty positive column and should not read that as evidence AI does not produce revenue.
entries.confidence_why: Primary abstract retrieved and quoted directly; paper body not read this run. Preprint, not yet peer reviewed. Secondary coverage (theaiinsider.tech, 14 Jul) additionally claims the study found 'little evidence that AI adoption was associated with higher revenue per employee' - that line is NOT in the abstract and is unverified against the paper body, so it is excluded from the claim above. Source is 17 days old, outside the trailing-48h window, logged as a strong prior-fortnight item.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (23 Jul 2026) CEO Vimal Kapur guided software ARR growth of ~15% for 2026 and said the business will "inch from about $900 million to a little over $1 billion of ARR in that segment this year." He described Forge as "the primary mechanism for delivering 'physical AI' to customers" and named software ARR as "the best way to measure our progress" toward autonomy. No revenue was attributed to AI itself.
entries.source_name: Honeywell Q2 2026 earnings call transcript (Motley Fool); 15% ARR figure corroborated in Investing.com transcript
entries.mechanism: Honeywell Forge is the connected-plant software layer sold on top of Honeywell's installed automation base (Kapur: "we have been selling automation since 1975"). It is sold as subscription ARR, and the AI/autonomy content is being positioned as the reason customers move up the subscription tiers. The revenue mechanism is software attach onto existing hardware relationships, not a new product with no predecessor.
entries.shape_justification: S2. Test: absent this AI capability, would the buyer have bought something similar from somebody? Yes - industrial asset-performance and process-optimization software is a contested category (AVEVA, Siemens, GE Vernova, ABB, Rockwell). Growth here is share taken inside an existing budget line, zero-sum at industry level and GDP-neutral. Explicitly NOT S3: Forge has a predecessor in Honeywell's own catalog going back years, and no capability gate at the 24-month frontier is established. The attribution weakness is the point of logging it: this is the largest AI-linked top-line number a non-tech industrial put on the record this quarter, and management still did not attribute a single dollar of it to AI - only to "Forge offerings" and "the launch of new software products." 'Physical AI' is the framing wrapped around a pre-existing software line.
entries.falsifier: Forge/segment software ARR failing to print above $1.0bn on the Q4 2026 / FY26 results, or the ~15% ARR growth rate not being restated on the Q3 2026 call. Second and sharper falsifier: if Honeywell never breaks out an AI-attributed revenue figure across FY26-FY27 while continuing to describe Forge as its physical-AI delivery mechanism, treat the AI framing as a repositioning of existing software revenue rather than an AI result.
entries.confidence_why: The 15% ARR growth guide is corroborated across two independent transcripts. The $900m-to-$1bn absolute figure was verified verbatim by direct retrieval but appears in only one transcript source, and Kapur's phrase "that segment" is not unambiguously tied to a named reporting segment in the retrieved text - do not treat the $900m base as an audited segment disclosure. Status is PROJECTED because it is a within-year guide, not a realized print.

entries.company: Grant Thornton 2026 AI Impact Survey - manufacturing cut (n=100 of 950)
entries.claim: Survey of 950 business leaders across 10 industries, fielded 23 Feb - 18 Mar 2026: "Among manufacturing respondents, zero reported significant revenue uplift from AI initiatives, compared to 12% of executives across all industries. Zero reported significant cost savings, again compared to 12% overall." 47% of manufacturers reported only minimal revenue uplift; 64% reported increased efficiency. Manufacturers led all sectors in operational AI deployment (62%) while reporting the weakest financial return.
entries.source_name: Grant Thornton, "Manufacturing insights: 2026 AI Impact Survey Report" (survey fielded 23 Feb - 18 Mar 2026; press coverage 9 Jul 2026)
entries.mechanism: Not a deployment finding - a base-rate measurement of the population this log samples from, and the cleanest available quantification of the efficiency-without-revenue gap: 64% report efficiency gains, 0% report significant revenue uplift, in the sector with the HIGHEST operational deployment rate. If efficiency mechanically converted to top line, the sector leading deployment should not be the sector reporting zero.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence, tagged to S2 because S2 (attributed incremental revenue on existing products) is the shape most non-tech corporates claim and the shape this null result most directly contradicts. It also constrains S3 by implication: a sector reporting zero significant revenue uplift is not opening new markets. The 58%-vs-15% headline elsewhere in the same survey (fully-integrated vs piloting firms reporting AI-driven revenue growth) is a selection-effect artifact, not causal evidence - firms that integrate deeply are firms that already saw something work - and should not be cited as offsetting the manufacturing zero.
entries.falsifier: The 2027 wave of the same survey showing manufacturing significant-revenue-uplift materially above zero, or a Q3/Q4 2026 cluster of named manufacturers disclosing AI-attributed revenue. Either would mean this reading was a timing artifact of a sector mid-J-curve rather than a structural absence.
entries.confidence_why: Tier D, and METHOD says Tier D is never the sole basis for an entry. Logged anyway with that conflict stated, on one specific ground: the systematic-inflation bias that justifies distrusting Tier D runs the OTHER WAY here - Grant Thornton sells AI advisory and is publishing a zero against its own commercial interest. Remaining limits are real: self-reported, non-random sample, "significant" undefined by the respondent, n=100 subgroup, and the field window (Feb-Mar 2026) is ~5 months stale relative to today. Age also exceeds the 14-day window; included because it is unlogged and directly load-bearing on the thesis.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (22 Jul 2026) CEO Trevor Burgess said the newly live quote-to-bind model is "definitely having a positive impact on the new business sales"; ~3,700 agents exchanged 33,000 messages with the Atlas+ assistant during the quarter. Q2 revenue $55.9m (+33% YoY), written premium $126.9m (+31%), lifetime written loss ratio 19.5%, FY26 revenue guided to $199m. None of the revenue is attributed to either system.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (22 Jul); figures corroborated by the 21 Jul results release
entries.mechanism: Two distinct systems in the revenue path. (1) A machine-learning quote-to-bind model inside Triton, the underwriting platform, scoring and routing submissions with no human underwriter in the loop. (2) Atlas+, an agent-facing assistant sitting on the quote screen answering the writing agent's questions in real time and drafting follow-up email, with a ranked next-best-task feed due in Q3. The stated route to revenue is higher agent quoting throughput and a better quote-to-bind conversion rate.
entries.shape_justification: S1, not S2 or S3. Every disclosed number is an input metric - agent count, message count - and the revenue statement is qualitative. Management gave a precise written-premium figure ($126.9m) and a precise FY guide ($199m) and attributed neither to the AI: this is the S1 conversion silence in its purest form, from a company that is otherwise unusually forthcoming. The S3 read was run and failed: >55% of new business outside mandatory flood zones and >75% voluntary purchase looks like new demand, but NFIP already writes voluntary policies outside the SFHA, so test (b) fails on prior alternative; and Burgess said flatly "We're not using AI to set pricing... All of the AI that we're using is algorithmic," which fails test (c) on the capability gate. Appendix, not main, because the subject is out of scope in its own words - the 21 Jul release calls Neptune an "AI-native managing general agent" that "operates without human underwriters." It does not test whether an ordinary incumbent gets revenue ROI from AI spend; it tests whether an AI-native entrant can take share in a boring line. Logged so that comparator stays visible rather than being discarded.
entries.falsifier: By the Q4 2026 / FY26 call, a disclosed quote-to-bind conversion delta or bound-premium dollar figure attributable to the model. If Atlas+ engagement counts keep growing across Q3 and Q4 while the conversion number never appears, the quote-to-bind claim was narrative and the 31-33% growth was distribution and pricing, not AI.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call, named executive, on-the-record quotes, and hard quarter figures from the results release - but zero of the revenue is AI-attributed, and an AI-native subject cannot test the incumbent thesis this log exists to test.

entries.claim: In the Q1 FY27 results release (23 Jul 2026) Infosys disclosed "AI as a % of Revenue" of 8.2% on total revenue of $5,082m (derived: approx. $417m), up from approximately 5.5% two quarters earlier. CEO Salil Parekh: "AI momentum is now rapidly converting into revenue, which demonstrates how Infosys' differentiated enterprise AI value proposition is translating into consistent market share gains." In the same release Infosys narrowed FY27 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to 1.5%-3.0% from 1.5%-3.5%, with reported growth of 2.4% YoY in constant currency.
entries.source_name: Infosys Q1 FY27 results release / Form 6-K, 23 Jul 2026; definition of the metric and the deflation commentary from Dataquest deep dive of the same call (Tier C, secondary)
entries.mechanism: Infosys sells AI-first services across six named value pools - AI strategy, process redesign, agents, data modernisation, AI engineering, platform-led implementation. Per Dataquest's account of the call, the metric deliberately EXCLUDES conventional engagements that merely have AI tools bolted onto existing workflows; those are tracked internally and not disclosed. That is a materially tighter definition than the 'AI-influenced revenue' constructs METHOD rejects, and it is the reason this is loggable at all. Running the other way, management described client pressure to use coding assistants and agents to complete existing work with fewer people and hours - reported as 'AI-led deflation' - compressing application maintenance, infrastructure operations and software development revenue, and said the two effects 'cannot always be separated cleanly' because clients bundle productivity concessions into contracts that also award new AI work.
entries.shape_justification: S2, and the CEO says so himself: 'market share gains'. Absent Infosys' AI capability these buyers would have bought transformation and engineering services from Accenture, TCS, Wipro, Cognizant or Capgemini - test (a) fails for S3, a competitor lost the sale. Test (c) is arguably passed (agentic delivery is a genuine post-2024 capability) but capability novelty alone does not make new demand. Zero-sum at industry level; GDP-neutral. Subject is out of scope for the main log in METHOD's own terms - an IT services firm selling AI implementation is a shovel vendor, and its AI revenue describes its own sales rather than a corporate's deployment ROI - so it is routed to the appendix and never counted. Flagged counter_evidence because the pairing is the finding: AI revenue share rose roughly 50% in two quarters and the company cut total growth guidance in the same release. Gross AI revenue up, net top line down. This is the sharpest quantification yet found of AI revenue substituting for the base rather than adding to it - and it comes from a firm whose whole business is selling AI, which is the population most incentivised to show the opposite.
entries.falsifier: If AI-first revenue share keeps climbing through FY27 (Q2 and Q3) while constant-currency total growth guidance stays at or below 3%, the substitution read is confirmed and the 8.2% is a mix metric, not a growth metric. Conversely, if total cc growth guidance is raised above 3% while AI share rises, AI revenue is genuinely additive and this entry is wrong. Second falsifier: if Infosys stops publishing 'AI as a % of Revenue' - a disclosure a company retires when the number stops flattering it.
entries.confidence_why: The 8.2%, the revenue base and the guidance are Tier A primary. The six-value-pool definition, the ~5.5% prior-quarter comparator and the 'AI-led deflation' language reach me only through one trade-press deep dive of the call, not the transcript itself - load-bearing and second-hand, so flagged.

days.assessment:
> **Zero findings in the main log for the second day running. No S3, no S3-CANDIDATE, and no non-tech corporate anywhere on the 27-29 Jul tape put a revenue number next to AI.** One appendix entry, and it is the most useful thing found this run precisely because it cuts against the thesis: Infosys disclosed AI revenue rising and total growth guidance falling in the same release.

## Sources read

- **Infosys** Q1 FY27 (23 Jul): `8.2%` of revenue is AI-first services on `$5,082m` (derived `~$417m`), up from `~5.5%` two quarters earlier - and FY27 constant-currency growth guidance *narrowed down* to `1.5-3.0%` from `1.5-3.5%` in the same release. Logged to the appendix. See below.
- **IQVIA** Q2 2026 (28 Jul): revenue `$4.368bn` `+8.7%`, R&D net new bookings `$3.15bn` `+19.3%`, book-to-bill `1.22`, backlog `$34.2bn`. AI content is entirely adoption counting - `294` agents across `90` use cases, `19 of the top 20` pharma have deployed IQVIA AI tools, `4 of the top 10` contracted to co-develop. Not one dollar of the record bookings is attributed to any of it. CFO Fedock: AI is *"just another lever in that toolkit."*
- **Ford** Q2 2026 (28 Jul): revenue `$48.3bn`; `1.6m` paid subscriptions, BlueCruise paid subs `+20%`, Ford Pro Intelligence `>900k` `+20%`, BlueCruise `50%` of retail Integrated Services revenue. Farley calls it *"our best proof point for software."* **Not called AI, and correctly so** - see near-misses.
- **Philips** Q2 2026 (28 Jul): group sales `EUR 4.4bn`, `+4%` comparable. Several AI-powered clearances in the quarter, SmartIQ cited at `>50%` less radiation. No AI revenue or order-intake breakout of any kind.
- **Hilton** Q2 2026 (28 Jul): RevPAR `+3.9%`, adjusted EBITDA `$1.054bn`. Exactly one AI mention on the call and it is about *other people's* datacentre capex as a source of travel demand. Nothing attributed.
- **AstraZeneca** Q2 2026 (27 Jul): **zero mentions of AI or machine learning in the entire transcript.** A top-five pharma, mid-AI-boom, discussing pipeline and timelines for an hour without using the word. Worth recording as its own data point.
- **T-Mobile** Q2 2026 (23 Jul): service revenue `+9%`, postpaid churn `0.85%`. First network-native AI application (live translation) shipped in beta; Dynamic CX ran during the World Cup. Framed explicitly as future opportunity, no revenue quantified.
- **Kinsale Capital** Q2 2026 (24 Jul): combined ratio `75.5%`, operating ROE `24.4%`. CFO frames AI as efficiency that *"could offset"* rising reinsurance commissions - cost side, out of scope by construction.
- **Goosehead Insurance** Q2 2026 (22 Jul): revenue `$113m` `+21%`, written premium `$1.36bn` `+14%`. Digital Agent 2.0 launched in Texas and described as *"the country's first true end-to-end choice shopping platform for personal lines"* - with no premium or revenue contribution disclosed and, on the read obtained, no use of the term AI at all.
- **Publicis Groupe** H1 2026 (16 Jul): Q2 organic `+4.8%`, Q1 `+4.5%`, FY guide raised to `+4.5-5.0%`, six major wins worth `~200bps`. Rejected - see near-misses.

> **Four days in, the pattern has stopped being a pattern and started being a finding.** Ten companies read this run, roughly twenty-five across four days, and the count of non-tech corporates that have voluntarily bridged an AI mention to a revenue number remains **zero**. The bridge is not missing because AI is absent from these calls - AI is on almost all of them. It is missing because attribution is either not measured or not survivable under disclosure liability. BCG's 22 Jul CEO survey puts a number on that same gap from the inside: only `14%` of 152 CEOs at `$500m+` companies have clearly defined P&L impact for all their AI initiatives.

## The appendix entry, and why it is the day's real signal

Infosys is out of scope as a subject - an IT services firm selling AI implementation is a shovel vendor, and its AI revenue is its own sales, not a corporate's deployment ROI. It goes to the appendix and is never counted. But it is the sharpest disclosure on the tape, for a reason that inverts the usual reading.

The metric is unusually honest by construction. Per Dataquest's deep dive of the call, `8.2%` covers six named value pools and **excludes** conventional engagements with AI tools bolted on - the exclusion that turns most AI-revenue metrics into the denominator games METHOD rejects. On that tighter definition AI revenue went from `~5.5%` to `8.2%` in two quarters.

And in the same release the company cut its growth guidance. Management named the mechanism - client pressure to deliver existing work with *"fewer people, fewer hours or lower costs"*, reported as **"AI-led deflation"** - and conceded the two effects *"cannot always be separated cleanly"* because clients bundle productivity concessions into the same contracts that award new AI work. HCLTech is cited in the same piece estimating portfolio deflation at `2-3%`; not logged, second-hand and undated.

> **Gross AI revenue up ~50% in two quarters; net top line guided down.** If the firm whose entire business model is selling AI cannot show AI as net additive to its own top line, the prior on non-tech incumbents showing it should fall, not rise. That is a harder constraint on the S2 story than any of the null surveys already in this log, because it comes from the party with the strongest incentive to report the opposite.

## Near-misses deliberately not logged

- **Publicis Groupe** - the CEO's claim that `87%` of net revenue is *"AI-powered marketing services"* is a denominator game of exactly the kind METHOD names, and the `~20%` three-year growth *"4 times faster than our competition"* is a comparative on a segment defined circularly as the AI-powered one. Decisive test: **the primary press release contains one AI sentence and attributes no growth to AI.** When the quantified AI claim exists only in the call narration and not in the printed release, that asymmetry is the tell. Note the three retrieved summaries disagreed on H1 organic growth (`4.7%` vs `5.3%` vs the release's `+4.8%` Q2 / `+4.5%` Q1) - a second reason to hold to the release.
- **Ford / BlueCruise** and **GM / Super Cruise** (carried from 28 Jul) - fail the same test (c). ADAS subscriptions are real new-SKU revenue and growing `+20%`, but the capability shipped in 2017-2021. Neither company calls it AI. Reading it as AI revenue would be attribution laundering performed by the reader, not the issuer.
- **IQVIA** - `294` agents, `90` use cases, `19 of 20` top pharma. Adoption counting, not a velocity metric and not revenue: a deployment census tells you nothing about throughput or hit rate. Also arguably out of scope as a subject. Fails the bar on the number, not on scope.
- **BCG CEO survey** (22 Jul, n=`152`, `$500m+` revenue) - the `14%`-defined-P&L-impact figure is quoted above because it corroborates the disclosure gap, but the headline (*"nearly nine in ten CEOs see cost or revenue benefits"*) is self-reported sentiment, no fielding date is given, and the log already holds two better-instrumented measurements of the same phenomenon. A third would be padding, not convergence.
- **Schneider Electric, Siemens, Nokia** - AI-attributed revenue that is datacentre and grid capex sold *into* the buildout. Shovel revenue. Same rejection as 28 Jul.
- **Agentic-commerce sweep** - returned only vendor and aggregator statistics again (conversion rates, referred-traffic shares). No named merchant disclosed a figure. Tier D, third run in a row it has come back empty.

## Nearest dated catalysts

- **Thu 30 - Fri 31 Jul:** back half of the non-tech Q2 tape. Insurers and consumer names still to print.
- **Thu 13 Aug: Heartflow Q2 2026** (confirmed date). AI-derived FFR-CT with its own reimbursement pathway is the single closest thing to a clean S3 on any calendar - a diagnostic sold to patients whose prior alternative was invasive angiography or nothing. Q1 revenue grew `41%` and guidance was raised. Whether it is in scope or appendix turns on how the company describes itself; the counterfactual tests should be run properly on that print.
- **Infosys Q2 FY27 (Oct):** does AI share keep rising while cc growth guidance stays at or below `3%`? That is this entry's falsifier and the cleanest near-term test of the substitution thesis.
- **CMS CY2027 payment rules:** still the clearest structural S3 enabler in view. Standing item until a named provider books revenue against a new AI code.
- **Neptune Q3 (Oct):** does a quote-to-bind conversion number ever appear? Carried from 28 Jul.

days.assessment:
> **Empty day in the main log — zero findings, no S3, not even a candidate.** Twenty search angles, six Q2 2026 transcripts read in full. One out-of-scope finding recorded in the appendix. The gap today was not a shortage of AI talk; it was that every AI mention arrived without a number attached to revenue, and every large revenue number arrived without AI attached to it.

## Sources read

- **UPS** 2Q 2026 release (28 Jul, the only in-window primary print reviewed): revenue `$22.8bn`, FY guide raised to `~$91.2bn`, `$1.2bn` of H1 transformation benefits — all attributed to *network reconfiguration and efficiency*, with **no AI attribution anywhere in the release**. A large logistics incumbent mid-transformation declining to put the AI label on its own savings is worth noting.
- **General Motors** Q2 2026: OnStar revenue `$800m`, `+20%` YoY; deferred revenue `$6.3bn`, up nearly `50%`; Super Cruise attach rate `30-40%`; `~1m` new subscriptions expected in 2026. The single largest genuinely-new-SKU revenue line found this run — and **GM does not call it AI.** Date discrepancy flagged: the call was 21 Jul, the OnStar detail surfaced in trade coverage dated 27 Jul.
- **Verizon** Q2 2026 (24 Jul): churn `84bps` (`-6bps` YoY), promo CAC `-15%`, Simplicity gross adds `16%` better than forecast. None of it attributed to AI. The AI-linked revenue is the Google dark-fibre deal — `>$1bn`, contributing "beginning in 2027." That is selling capacity *to* the buildout, not ROI *from* deployment.
- **BNY** Q2 2026 (22 Jul): `~40%` of engineer-written software now AI-generated; management calls AI "a capacity creator," says impact is "tangible, and measurable" — and then **discloses no measure.** AI spend inside the `$4bn` engineering budget described as "de minimis."
- **The Hartford** Q2 2026 (24 Jul): underwriting activities "completed in a fraction of the time"; small-business written premium `+7%`. The `7%` is not attributed to the AI and the "fraction" is not quantified. Fails the bar on both halves.
- **Intuitive Surgical** Q2 2026 (17 Jul): revenue `$2.89bn` `+19%`, recurring `85%` of total. Exactly **one** AI sentence in the entire call, listing it among R&D domains. No standalone disclosure for Case Insights or Intuitive Hub.
- **Neptune Insurance** Q2 2026 (release 21 Jul, call 22 Jul): revenue `$55.9m` `+33%`, written premium `$126.9m` `+31%`, loss ratio `19.5%`, FY26 guide `$199m`. Logged to the appendix — see below.

> **The pattern, three days in: the disclosure gap is not random — it is structural.** Where AI is named, no number follows; where a number is disclosed, AI is not named. Seven calls this run, and not one company voluntarily bridged the two. Firms quantify what they are proud of and what investors demand; AI revenue attribution is so far in neither category. That silence is the finding, and it is repeating.

## Appendix entry, and the schema change behind it

**Neptune Insurance** is the sharpest disclosure found today and it sat outside the schema. It is logged to the appendix under a rule change made this run: `scope: appendix` now accepts **any** shape, not S3 only. The original S3-only constraint would have discarded a quantified S1 from a Tier A call — the wrong failure, because an entrant's S1 is the natural comparator for the incumbent silence catalogued above. Neptune is out of scope in its own words (an *"AI-native managing general agent"* that *"operates without human underwriters"*), so it is never counted in the totals; it is kept visible so the incumbent-vs-entrant split stays measurable.

The S3 read on Neptune was run and failed on two independent tests, which is worth recording because it is the single most gameable claim in this sector: `>55%` of new business outside mandatory flood zones and `>75%` voluntary purchase looks like new demand, but **NFIP already writes voluntary policies outside the SFHA** — test (b) fails — and Burgess said flatly *"We're not using AI to set pricing... All of the AI that we're using is algorithmic"* — test (c) fails. A company growing `33%` with AI in its self-description, and its own CEO closing off the capability-gate argument.

## Near-misses deliberately not logged

- **GM / Super Cruise** — fails test (c) hard. Super Cruise shipped in 2017; the `+20%` OnStar growth is distribution expansion across more equipped models, not a frontier capability jump. Logging it as AI revenue would be attribution laundering of exactly the kind METHOD warns about. Note that GM itself is not making the claim — the temptation here is entirely on the reader's side.
- **Nokia** Q2 2026 — "AI sales surge `105%`." Reject: telecom-equipment revenue sold *into* AI datacentre capex. Shovel revenue, not deployment ROI. Same rejection applies to the big-bank fee income from SpaceX-style AI megadeals.
- **Massimo Group** — `$19.7m` / up-to-5,000-unit commitment for a "new AI-enabled product category." Reject on four counts: dated 13 Jan 2026 (out of window), counterparty unnamed, product undisclosed, and the company states revenue recognition "remain[s] subject to various contingencies." A micro-cap LOI is not a result.
- **AIG / Great American / W.R. Berkley AI-liability exclusions** — real counter-evidence to the "insurers open new TAM by pricing AI risk" thesis, but the filings are Nov 2025 and the reporting April 2026. Too stale to log as new; carried forward as a standing signal.
- **Agentic-commerce and AI-drive-thru sweeps** — returned only vendor and consultancy material. No deploying company disclosed a referred-sales or check-average figure. Tier D, not logged.

## The week's non-tech Q2 prints

Strikingly consistent — AI is discussed everywhere, quantified nowhere on the revenue line.

- **Verizon** — separates AI-for-operations (cost) from AI Connect (revenue) and puts the revenue in **2027**. Its `$1bn` Google dark-fiber deal is demand from the AI buildout, not ROI on Verizon's own AI spend — out of frame for this log.
- **SLB** — Digital division `$697m`, **+18% y/y**; ARR `$1.04bn`, **+15%**. But management bundles AI inside Delfi/Lumi/Agora/Tela and isolates no AI-specific figure, so the growth number cannot be attributed.
- **Halliburton** — names Zeus iQ, LOGIX and the Sekal acquisition as automation differentiators, **no dollar attached**.
- **Delta** — mentions "AI-powered personalization" once, unquantified. Its Fetcherr pricing work is under political scrutiny and Delta's own on-record statement **declines to give any percentage** of fares or revenue effect.

## Rejected on method rather than substance

- **RELX** (H1 2026, 23 Jul) — disclosed that **~90% of new sales value** and ~three-quarters of renewal value in Legal now runs through the AI-enabled Lexis+/Protégé platform, against 10% underlying Legal growth. That is the **denominator game** METHOD names explicitly: AI-touched share of bookings is not incremental revenue. RELX's subject status is borderline anyway.
- **PwC 2026 AI performance study** and **FMI grocery technology survey** — consultant/trade sentiment, no named company.
- **AWS 3.5x shopping-assistant conversion claim** — Tier D vendor, tech subject.
- **Munich Re aiSure** and the **Beazley–AIUC AI liability paper** — genuinely new insurance classes, but they are demand created by *other people's* AI risk, not revenue from the insurer's own AI deployment, and no premium figure is disclosed.

## The signal: Albertsons

In January the CEO put a specific, checkable revenue-side number on the record — **Ask AI delivering a 10% basket-size lift**.

Six months later, on 23 July, the same CEO reaffirmed AI as foundational, laid out four enterprise AI priorities (**three of them cost-side**), guided `$1.9–2.0bn` of capex toward stores and AI — and gave **no AI-attributed revenue metric at all**. Digital sales grew 13%, unattributed.

> **Companies repeat numbers that are working.** The disclosure asymmetry — specific quantified cost and productivity metrics from BofA, specific quantified capex from Albertsons, and qualitative adjectives everywhere the revenue line should be — is the actual pattern across every non-tech Q2 print read today, and it is what this log exists to measure.

No new positive findings; one further counter-evidence entry added.

- **Honeywell** — Q2 call contains no substantive AI discussion at all. Its datacenter exposure is sold as fire, security, on-site power and liquid cooling: demand *from* the AI buildout, not AI deployed to produce revenue.
- **Roche** — H1 gives two AI mentions, both forward-looking: the PathAI acquisition in digital pathology, and a promise to address AI in early drug development at Pharma Day on 28 Sep 2026. No revenue, no timeline, no addressable-population number.
- **Mechanism-term sweep** (quote-to-bind, attach rate, next-best-action, retail media, hotel yield management) returned vendor marketing exclusively, with no carrier, retailer or operator putting its own number on the record.

## The confound worth naming

The added **MIT FutureTech / CMU** 10-K adoption study reframes the empty positive column. Two-thirds of deeply integrated enterprise AI adoption sits in the technology sector; non-tech adoption is described as only *slowly accelerating*. This log excludes tech as subjects by design, so **it is sampling the thin end of the distribution**.

That is a real confound: an empty log is consistent both with *"AI does not yet produce measurable top-line revenue at incumbents"* and with *"incumbents have not yet deeply adopted it"* — and nothing found today distinguishes the two. The falsifier on that entry is written to force the distinction over the next two 10-K vintages.

**Noted for method:** the entry breaches inclusion-bar rule 1 (named company), because no aggregate study can satisfy it, while the counter-evidence clause explicitly names null studies as loggable. Those two rules conflict; this run resolved in favour of the counter-evidence clause.
